Geophysicist chiming in. It's an interesting and rather complex mechanism actually. Simplified to the bare minimum, it goes something like this:

The inner core is solid, the outer core is liquid, both are made up of mostly iron. As the planet slowly cools, the outer layers become colder than the lower layers.

Due to this temperature difference, convection in the outer core carries heat from the IC to the mantle. As heat is lost, part of the liquid solidifies and the IC slowly grows. But solidifying releases heat, and this heat keeps the IC warm while offering energy to keep convection going.

Now you have convective currents of iron in the outer core. If this metallic liquid flows through a magnetic field, it will generate electric currents. And these electric currents generate a stronger magnetic field.

This self-stabilizes at a certain point. Convective currents are (mostly) powered by the temperature difference between inner core and mantle, further powered by the growing inner core. These generate electric currents, which generate a magnetic field which again influences the electric currents.

And while a (mostly) dipolar field will (roughly) align with the planetary axis of rotation, there is no preferred direction for north or south.

Now why it flips is basically a coupled oscillator system. When the mass distribution is such that north or south is more preferable to align the field with, it's stable. When they become comparable in stability, we enter a period of oscillations. North dipole, quadrupole, south dipole, quadrupole, north dipole, ... Until the mantle and plates shift again and the mass distribution stabilizes the field one way or the other again.
